<SUMMARY>The week of May 22-29, 2026, was dominated by intensified competition in the AI and semiconductor sectors, marked by significant investments and escalating US export controls. NVIDIA unveiled its Vera CPU and committed substantial investment to Taiwan, while SoftBank Group pledged EUR75 billion for AI data centers in France. The US Commerce Department expanded export controls to prevent advanced AI chips, including NVIDIA's Blackwell processors, from reaching Chinese firms through overseas subsidiaries. Geopolitical tensions in West Asia escalated with direct military engagements between the US and Iran, alongside expanded Israeli military operations in Lebanon, impacting global oil markets and supply chains. The global race for critical minerals saw new agreements and enforcement actions, with the US securing a rare earth deal in Greenland and African nations taking steps against illegal mining, while India sought critical minerals from Chile and rare earths from Myanmar.</SUMMARY>
<EWS>Escalating US-Iran military actions, including an alleged F-15E shootdown and reciprocal strikes, signal a high potential for broader conflict in West Asia, impacting oil supply and regional stability. The US tightening of AI chip export controls to Chinese firms overseas highlights a sustained and expanding technological containment strategy, increasing bifurcation risks for the global semiconductor supply chain. The disruption of West Asia supply chains due to the Iran conflict is prompting Indian consumer goods firms to reroute manufacturing and sourcing, indicating a regional risk to global trade.</EWS>
<EXEC>Global AI development continues to drive significant investment, with NVIDIA introducing the Vera CPU and securing strategic partnerships. Jensen Huang announced plans to invest around $150 billion a year in Taiwan, describing it as the epicenter of the AI revolution, and praised Taiwan as the "World's Best Supply Chain". SoftBank Group committed up to EUR75 billion to develop 5GW of AI data center capacity in France. Intel plans to launch an AI chip by year-end with lower-cost technology. The US Commerce Department expanded export controls to prevent Chinese technology companies from obtaining advanced AI chips, including NVIDIA's Blackwell processors, through overseas subsidiaries. Huawei's chairman, however, stated that US export restrictions have supercharged China’s semiconductor industry, encouraging domestic R&D.

**Asia:**
NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang announced plans to invest around $150 billion a year in Taiwan, describing it as the epicenter of the AI revolution. Jensen Huang praised Taiwan as the "World's Best Supply Chain."

**Europe:**
SoftBank Group announced it will invest as much as EUR75 billion (US$87.43 billion) to develop 5GW of AI data center capacity in France, aiming to establish the country as one of its largest AI infrastructure bases in Europe. The first phase targets 3.1GW in the Hauts-de-France region by 2029. SoftBank Group also announced on May 31st that it will build a data center in France dedicated to artificial intelligence, with total investment potentially reaching approximately 14 trillion yen.</EXEC>
<LITHO>
**Asia:**
US export controls and the denial of EUV lithography equipment have effectively capped China's front-end chip manufacturing.

**Europe:**
Nikon is leveraging in-house manufacturing to slash prices, aiming to break ASML's lithography monopoly and attract American chipmakers.
</LITHO>
<REE>
**Africa:**
The Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod) announced the procurement of 10 high-tech speedboats for the National Anti-Illegal Mining Operational Secretariat (NAIMOS) to combat illegal mining. The NSCDC arraigned 15 Chinese nationals and nine Nigerians in Abuja for alleged illegal lithium mining in Nasarawa State. Africa faces new competition for critical minerals investment as the U.S. secured a rare earth deal in Greenland, aiming to reduce reliance on China.

**Americas:**
Brazil is seeing increased demand for its vast reserves of rare earth elements, with global mining giants investing to develop it as an alternative to China's dominance in critical magnetic metals.

**Oceania:**
Rio Tinto Group reported that its aluminum shipments to the US have rebounded to levels from before President Donald Trump’s tariff offensive.</REE>
<GEO>
**Asia:**
The US Commerce Department moved to close an export-control loophole that may have allowed Chinese technology companies to obtain advanced AI chips, including NVIDIA's Blackwell processors, through subsidiaries outside China. Taiwan secured preferential treatment under US Section 232 tariffs for most exports other than semiconductors after months of negotiations with Washington. Huawei's chairman stated that US export restrictions have supercharged China’s semiconductor industry, encouraging investment in R&D and building domestic tech stack competing with American tech. The US confirmed that its ban on AI chip shipments applies to Chinese firms outside China, issuing guidance on chip restrictions amid concerns about loopholes in the export control regime.

**Americas:**
Rio Tinto Group reported its shipments of aluminum to the US have bounced back to levels from before President Donald Trump’s tariff offensive.

**Europe:**
The aluminum associations of the United States, Europe, Canada, and Japan welcomed the release by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) of new data on industrial subsidies.</GEO>
<MILITARY>
**Asia:**
A blast in Shan state's Namhkam district, northern Myanmar, killed dozens, with rebels controlling the region stating it was caused by the accidental detonation of mining explosives. Russia signed a military cooperation deal with Afghanistan's Taliban Government. Türkiye expressed eagerness to cooperate with Japan in the field of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).

**Europe:**
Ukrainian drones struck a Russian refinery deep behind front lines.</MILITARY>
<CONCLUSION>Global AI market leadership remains a key strategic competition, marked by significant investments from NVIDIA and SoftBank, and an intensifying technological containment strategy by the US targeting China's access to advanced AI chips. The expansion of US export controls to overseas Chinese entities underscores a hardening stance. The West Asia region remains highly volatile, with direct military engagements between the US and Iran, coupled with Israeli military expansion in Lebanon, driving oil price fluctuations and supply chain disruptions. This ongoing instability has prompted regional and international actors to reassess strategic resource dependencies and supply chain resilience. The critical minerals sector is witnessing a global scramble for resources and diversification of supply chains, with African nations becoming pivotal sites for both extraction and geopolitical competition, and other nations like Brazil emerging as alternatives to China's rare earth dominance.</CONCLUSION>

<INDIA>Tomoe Shokai plans to launch a new factory in Gujarat in the 2027 fiscal year to produce medical treatment gas and facilities, citing India’s economic progress. Intel plans a US$3.3 billion India Substrate Plant, which redraws the AI supply chain. Indian semiconductor startups like Netrasemi, Mindgrove, and Agnit are nearing commercial production, with some already running customer pilots and aiming for large-scale output by late 2027, supported by government incentives. The semiconductor plant at Jagiroad in Assam is expected to start production within this financial year, according to I&B and Electronics and IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw. Anthropic is scaling its India leadership to capture enterprise demand. NITI Aayog urged India to prioritize chip design, OSAT, and advanced packaging over the foundry "wafer race," targeting a $120–150 billion value chain by 2035. Chile is offering India significant opportunities in critical mineral mining, including copper, lithium, and cobalt, and seeks Indian talent for its burgeoning semiconductor sector. Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing's visit to India presents a significant opportunity for New Delhi to secure rare earth minerals from Myanmar. Indian consumer goods firms like Dabur, Britannia, Tata Consumer Products, and Emami are rerouting manufacturing and sourcing away from West Asia due to the Iran conflict and Strait of Hormuz disruptions, shifting production to India, Egypt, and other locations. Former Foreign Secretary of India Kanwal Sibal discussed India’s diplomatic balancing acts amidst the widening crisis in West Asia as the Trump administration escalates confrontation with Iran.</INDIA>
<WEST_ASIA>Oil prices climbed as a US-Iran ceasefire deal remained elusive. US officials said a Chinese shoulder-fired MANPADS missile was possibly the weapon used to shoot down a US F-15E Strike Eagle over Iran, and are investigating this possibility. The United States launched strikes against Iranian radar and drone command sites in Goruk and on Qeshm Island after Tehran allegedly shot down a US MQ-1 drone over international waters. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) retaliated against the base from which the US attacked an Iranian island, according to Mehr news agency reports. The UN Security Council will hold an emergency meeting on Lebanon after Israel’s military took over Beaufort castle, escalating the conflict. Crude oil futures rose after Israel ordered an expansion of military operations in Lebanon, signaling potential market impacts amid regional tensions. The Iran conflict has disrupted oil supply, prompting Gulf states to explore multi-billion-dollar investments in renewables. The US and Iran are weighing an extension of their ceasefire by two weeks. Indian consumer goods firms are rerouting manufacturing and sourcing away from West Asia due to the Iran conflict and Strait of Hormuz disruptions.</WEST_ASIA>
<FINAL_CONCLUSION>The next quarter will likely see a continued intensification of technological competition, with US export controls continuing to shape global semiconductor supply chains and potentially driving further innovation within targeted nations. The instability in West Asia, particularly the US-Iran dynamic and the Israeli-Lebanese conflict, poses an ongoing risk to global energy markets and supply chains, necessitating adaptive strategies from international businesses. The global competition for critical minerals is set to accelerate, particularly as nations seek to diversify away from current monopolies to secure their green energy and advanced technology ambitions.</FINAL_CONCLUSION>
